\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Vision token pruning is one of the most reliable efficiency techniques in Vision Transformer (ViT) inference: DynamicViT~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit} removes 66\% of tokens with $<$0.5\% accuracy loss, ToMe~\cite{bolya2023tome} merges 40\% at $>$99\% accuracy, and EViT~\cite{liang2022evit} discards 50\% with negligible degradation. These results have established a strong prior that vision tokens are highly redundant. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~\cite{brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,ghosh2024octo,shukor2025smolvla} use the same ViT encoders, producing hundreds of tokens that dominate the LLM backbone's input. For real-time robotic control at 5--10 Hz, reducing these tokens would yield immediate speedups in the quadratically scaling attention computation. Several recent works explore this direction: FastV~\cite{chen2024fastv} prunes inattentive VLM tokens, VLA-Cache~\cite{xu2025vlacache} caches vision tokens across timesteps, and VLA-IAP~\cite{cheng2026vlaiap} proposes importance-aware VLA pruning.

However, no prior work has systematically evaluated how vision token reduction behaves across different VLA architectures in closed-loop control, where a single corrupted action can push the robot off-trajectory and subsequent errors compound irrecoverably. Existing evaluations rely on offline metrics (action loss, perplexity) that average over independent timesteps and fail to capture this compounding failure mode.

We conduct the first cross-architecture closed-loop evaluation. On SmolVLA (451.5M parameters, pixel-shuffle connector), seven pruning configurations spanning scoring function, retention ratio ($k \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$), and mechanism (zero-masking, true removal, token merging) all collapse to 0\% Success Rate (SR) across 500 episodes (Wilson 95\% CI: [0\%, 0.76\%]), even when retaining 95\% of tokens. The official SmolVLA checkpoint (59.2\% baseline) exhibits the same cliff-edge, confirming the failure is architectural. On OpenVLA (7B parameters, MLP projector), the same 50\% random removal yields 37.4\% SR against a 74.0\% baseline, with graded, task-dependent degradation. The key architectural difference is the vision connector: SmolVLA's pixel-shuffle folds $4{\times}4$ patches into high-density tokens with near-uniform attention (entropy ratio 0.98), while OpenVLA's MLP projector preserves per-token independence with selective deep-layer attention (entropy ratio 0.64). For architectures where pruning fails, we train a cross-attention module (Smart Compress) that re-encodes rather than deletes tokens, achieving 61.6\% SR at 75\% token reduction, a performance-neutral deployment benefit.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Architecture-dependent compressibility} (\S\ref{sec:results}): Pixel-shuffle connectors exhibit cliff-edge failure (59.2\% $\to$ 0\%); MLP projectors degrade gracefully (74.0\% $\to$ 37.4\%), consistent across three models and two connector families~\cite{yang2025efficientvla}.
\item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation} (\S\ref{sec:analysis}): The attention entropy ratio (0.98 vs.\ 0.64) captures the divergence and may serve as a preliminary compressibility signal.
\item \textbf{Cross-attention re-encoding} (\S\ref{sec:smart_compress_results}): Raises SR from 44.8\% to $\sim$60\% through re-encoding; 75\% token reduction preserves this gain at 61.6\%.
\item \textbf{Offline metric disconnect} (\S\ref{sec:metric_disconnect}): Standard offline proxies provide misleadingly optimistic estimates; closed-loop evaluation is essential.
\end{enumerate}
